extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, journalists, and educated readers interested in style and conversation
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance for writers and conversationalists on clarity, tone, economy, use of analogy, and journalistic ethics as articulated in an 18th‑century essayistic voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-writer ethics / truthfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: To write news in its perfection requires such a combination of qualities, that a man completely fitted for the task is not always to be found... contempt of shame and indifference to truth are absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: fabricating letters to oneself, asserting contradictory claims day to day, inventing battles or exaggerated atrocities to please readers. During war, news-writers tend to pander to national bias (telling good of ourselves and ill of the enemy) and manufacture sensational cruelty stories; avoid these practices. Emphasizes journalistic integrity over profit and sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for depth rather than mere readability/popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the amusements of idleness is reading without the fatigue of close attention, and the world therefore swarms with writers whose wish is not to be studied, but to be read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer work that rewards close study rather than cheap, ephemeral pieces designed only for easy consumption. Anti-pattern: writing that seeks only to be read superficially and immediately popular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize clarity over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man speaks and writes with intent to be understood; and it can seldom happen but he that understands himself, might convey his notions to another, if, content to be understood, he did not seek to be admired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not contrive sentences primarily to impress — clarity should be the central aim. If you understand yourself, write so others can understand you. Anti-patterns: ornament that sacrifices intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and directness (find the nearest way)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the nearest way from truth to truth, or from purpose to effect, not to use more instruments where fewer will be sufficient; not to move by wheels and levers what will give way to the naked hand, is the great proof of a healthful and vigorous mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for concision and direct methods of expression or argument. Avoid overcomplicating explanations or using elaborate devices when simple ones suffice. This applies to structure, argument, and rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'terrifick' or 'bugbear' style that obscures simple truths
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mode of style... by which the most evident truths are so obscured that they can no longer be perceived... This style may be called the terrifick... or the bugbear style, for it has more terrour than danger, and will appear less formidable as it is more nearly approached.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: abstruse, grandiose diction and scholastic obscurity that transform clear propositions into incomprehensible statements. Example: needlessly scholastic rephrasing of simple truths ('two and two make four' turned into elaborate metaphysical language). Avoid obscuring rather than illuminating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid self-defeating stylistic excesses
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a mode of style... the man of exuberance and copiousness... the ponderous dictator of sentences..., the liberal illustrator..., and the stately son of demonstration...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of specific counterproductive writing types: (a) Excessive verbosity that diffuses thought; (b) Overly ponderous, dense sentences that are heavy but not useful; (c) Overuse of examples and comparisons that state what was already clear; (d) Rigid, overly formal proofs of trivial points. These styles obscure rather than help comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary novelty or affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are men who seem to think nothing so much the characteristick of a genius, as to do common things in an uncommon manner... to quit the beaten track, only because it is known, and take a new path... because the straight was found out before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pursue novelty for its own sake. If a straightforward means communicates the idea best, use it. Affectation of originality that hinders comprehension is a vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and resemblance to instruct — but prefer literal parallels when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: To illustrate one thing by its resemblance to another, has been always the most popular and efficacious art of instruction... some are literal and real... others are fortuitous and fanciful, yet these have sometimes been extended... The former is more easily and generally understood; the latter have more of genius, but less of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose analogies that genuinely illuminate (literal/metaphorical choices that map well). Prefer comparisons grounded in real similarity for clarity; fanciful parallels may please but can fail to convince or mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance elements of tone in conversation and prose (the 'punch' formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punch... spirit (vivacity and wit), acidity (pungency of raillery), sugar (luscious adulation and gentle complaisance), and water (easy prattle). He only will please long, who, by tempering the acidity of satire with the sugar of civility, and allaying the heat of wit with the frigidity of humble chat, can make the true punch of conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dialogue and stylistic tone, blend vivacity and wit with civility, and temper sharpness with gentleness. Plain, unadorned diction (water) is the best base for conveying information; wit and raillery should be used sparingly and tempered so as not to overwhelm the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain diction as the primary vehicle for conveying knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Water is the only ingredient in punch which can be used alone... while we only desire to have our ignorance informed, we are most delighted with the plainest diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is to inform or teach, use simple, direct language. Reserve wit and ornament for moments when they add value rather than distract from comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of superficial familiarity masquerading as knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgar and inactive minds confound familiarity with knowledge, and conceive themselves informed of the whole nature of things when they are shown their form or told their use; but the speculatist... as he inquires more, perceives only that he knows less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigation should move beyond mere acquaintance with forms or uses; deep understanding requires inquiry. Avoid assuming that surface familiarity constitutes true knowledge — this affects how convincingly one can write or argue about subjects.
